label: Falling ice from towers, turbines and buildings
summary: Freezing rain and icing in low cloud coat towers, guy wires, wind turbines, power lines, signs and building edges with ice. It falls as the air warms toward 0 °C or the structure moves, sometimes days later. A 0.2 kg piece falling 30–50 m can kill; ice thrown off turning blades can weigh kilograms.
signs: Ice on power lines, trees or fences: iced power lines may mean turbines nearby carry ice too
A thaw: temperatures rising to near or above 0 °C after an icing; ice can hang on for days after the storm
Ice chunks and craters in the snow around the base of a tower, mast or turbine
Icicles and snow hanging over roof edges, ledges, awnings and signs
A stopped wind turbine with ice on its blades or nacelle; a turning one throws ice much farther
Wind blowing from the structure toward you: falling ice drifts downwind, farther in stronger wind
Very heavy ice on lines and towers: in the worst ice storms, poles and towers collapse
do: Stay out of the fall zone until the ice is gone. Around a mast, tower or other structure, that is about 1.5 times its height from the base

Stopped turbine: ice can land up to the blade-tip height (hub height plus half the rotor) times the wind speed in m/s, divided by 15. In a 54 km/h (15 m/s) wind that is one tip height. A turning turbine can throw ice 1.5 × (rotor diameter + hub height)
Look the structure over before you go near it, come in from the upwind side, and keep your time close to it short
Have one person watch for falling ice while the others work, and park vehicles outside the fall zone

Near buildings, look at the roof before you approach and spend as little time beside the walls as you can, especially once it is warmer than about −5 °C. If the ice or snow looks unstable, keep people out of that area
If ice is coming down when you want to leave a building, hut or tower, stay inside until it stops
After an ice storm, watch overhead for ice-loaded branches and lines, which can break and fall
dont: Don't stand or park under iced towers, guy wires, turbine blades, signs or roof edges on a thaw day
Don't knock snow or ice off a roof while standing on the ground below it: it can all come down at once
Don't slam doors or bang on an iced structure: small vibrations can bring the ice down
Don't open a turbine hatch or go onto the nacelle while there is ice on it
ppe: A hard hat near any iced structure. It takes one blow and is the last line of defence; staying out of the fall zone is the real protection
Insulated safety boots with good grip: watch for ice patches on the ground
firstAid: Before you go to someone who was hit, look up and check what ice is still hanging
After a blow to the head, a headache that gets worse, repeated vomiting, slurred speech, confusion, one pupil bigger than the other, or drowsiness means urgent medical care
For neck and back injuries and moving a casualty, see Fall from height; to keep someone lying in snow warm, see Cold
